module.title: Present Perfect Continuous: Ongoing Actions vs Finished Results
module.objective: Membedakan aksi yang telah berlangsung hingga sekarang (have been doing) dengan hasil akhir aksi (have done).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Ongoing Actions and Finished Results
subModules.grammarFocus: Present Perfect Continuous vs Present Perfect Simple

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore how writers describe ongoing activities and finished results in everyday situations. You will learn to spot the difference between actions that continue up to the present moment and tasks that are already complete, improving your ability to understand texts about hobbies, studies, and personal projects.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Perfect Continuous (have/has been + verb-ing) contrasted with Present Perfect Simple for results.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words related to effort, duration, concentration, and progress in daily life.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific time expressions like for, since, lately, and recently to understand the duration of actions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about personal projects and hobbies.
Locate specific details regarding how long actions have been happening.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with the Present Perfect Continuous.

contextWarmup.prompt: If your friend looks very tired and has paint on their clothes, what are they likely to have been doing?
options: They have been painting the living room walls all morning.
They have been sleeping peacefully in their bed.
They have been reading a book in the quiet library.
contextWarmup.explanation: Paint on clothes and physical tiredness are strong visual evidence of an ongoing or just-finished physical activity like painting a room.

rules: Formula: Subject + have/has + been + verb-ing. Used for activities that started in the past and are still continuing or have just stopped with present evidence.
Common time expressions include for (duration), since (starting point), all morning, lately, recently, and how long.
Present Perfect Simple emphasizes the completed result (have done), while Present Perfect Continuous emphasizes the process and duration (have been doing).

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use the continuous form when talking about a finished quantity or a final result, forgetting that continuous focuses on the activity itself.
commonTrap.wrong: I have been writing three emails this morning.
commonTrap.correct: I have written three emails this morning. (Use simple for completed quantities).

paragraphs: It is Saturday afternoon, and Leo is sitting in the living room surrounded by art supplies. His hands are covered in blue paint, and there are sketches scattered all over the table. He looks exhausted but happy. Leo has been painting his bedroom mural since early morning. Because he has been working on it for over six hours, he has completed two main walls so far. However, he still has one more wall to finish before tomorrow evening.

Meanwhile, in the kitchen, Leo's sister Maya has been baking cookies. The wonderful smell of chocolate fills the whole house. Maya has been practicing her baking skills recently because she wants to enter a local food competition next month. She has already baked three different batches today, and she says her recipes have been improving steadily thanks to her new cookbook.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Present Perfect Continuous and Finished Results

content.summary: Practical guide on contrasting ongoing actions with finished results using the Present Perfect tense family in English paragraphs.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Ongoing Action Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have/has + been + verb-ing + duration clause
blueprintItems.example: She has been studying for three hours.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Finished Result Formula
blueprintItems.example: She has written three formal reports today.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Combining Duration and Result
blueprintItems.formula: Ongoing action sentence + connective + finished result sentence
blueprintItems.example: I have been painting the kitchen all morning, and now the walls look bright and clean.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'for' with a time period and 'since' with a specific starting point.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He has been working here since five years.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He has been working here for five years.
mechanicsRules.why: We measure duration with 'for' and state starting points with 'since'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use continuous verbs for permanent states or non-action verbs like know, want, or like.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I have been knowing him for a long time.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I have known him for a long time.
mechanicsRules.why: State verbs do not take the continuous form even when talking about duration up to now.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of every new sentence and use a period at the end.
mechanicsRules.badExample: they have been cleaning the lab all day. now it is tidy.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: They have been cleaning the lab all day. Now it is tidy.
mechanicsRules.why: Standard sentence boundaries require proper capitalization and terminal punctuation.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Present Perfect Continuous: Ongoing Actions vs Finished Results

content.summary: Mastering the contrast between ongoing actions using the Present Perfect Continuous and completed actions using the Present Perfect Simple requires careful attention to weak forms, auxiliary stress, and natural breathing pauses. When speaking at a B1 level, linking auxiliary verbs like 'have' and 'has' with pronouns and the word 'been' helps create fluent, natural speech.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on unstressed pronunciation of 'have been' as /həv bɪn/ or /həv biːn/, letting the main lexical verb carry the primary stress and tone. Contrast this with finished results where the past participle receives clear vocal prominence.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Weak Forms
pillars.target: Pronounce 'have' and 'has' as weak forms in continuous statements
pillars.explanation: In fast spoken English, 'have been' sounds like 'iv bin' or 'əv bɪn', allowing listeners to focus on the active verb ending in -ing.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress Contrast
pillars.target: Emphasize duration words versus completion quantities
pillars.explanation: When discussing ongoing actions, stress the duration phrase such as 'all morning' or 'for three hours'. When discussing finished results, stress the exact number of completed items.

pillars.name: Intonation in Clarifications
pillars.target: Use rising intonation when asking about ongoing duration and falling intonation when stating facts
pillars.explanation: Questions starting with 'How long have you been' require a rising pitch at the end to invite detailed explanations of ongoing activities.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity in Endings
pillars.target: Maintain clear schwa sounds in unstressed syllables
pillars.explanation: Ensure endings like 'recently', 'lately', and 'progress' are pronounced with precise vowel sounds rather than swallowed completely.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the primary stress moves to the second syllable when adding the suffix to form the continuous verb.
The noun places stress on the first syllable, whereas the verb places stress on the second syllable.
The stress remains on the second syllable in both the base verb and the continuous participle form.
The second syllable maintains primary stress while the ending adds an unstressed syllable.
